altyazi.metin: This solar panel...
was once a handful of sand!
From sand to electricity, here's the
journey.
It all starts with quartz.
Silicon is the second most abundant
element in Earth's crust, after oxygen.
Quartz is melted with carbon in an arc
furnace at nearly two thousand degrees.
Then it's purified until fewer than one
in a million atoms is an impurity.
A tiny seed crystal is dipped into
silicon melted at over fourteen hundred
degrees. Rotated and slowly pulled up...
a single-crystal ingot grows.
The ingot is sliced with diamond-coated
wires. Each slice is just 0.15
millimeters thick!
The slices are textured, doped and
coated, becoming cells.
Silver lines collect the electricity.
Cells are connected, then sealed with
glass, protective layers and an aluminum
frame. Now it's a panel.
Stacked on pallets, they cross oceans in
containers and reach the site by truck.
On site, piles are driven, the structure
is built, panels are mounted one by one,
and cables are laid.
And the sun rises. Light hits the cell,
electrons start moving.
The inverter converts the current...
and electricity flows into the grid.
Over twenty-five years of power, burning
no fuel. All from a handful of sand.
Follow Kozmos Lab!
